title: Progress in Georgia and music breaking barriers
summary: He and Willard discuss changes in Georgia, music breaking barriers, and friends on both sides in the South.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, I understand that amazing things are happening in Georgia.

Well, that's good. It's good to hear those things that they're turning around, you know. Things are kind of turning around because with the musicians, they don't like -- they don't like those things happening like that, you know. Macou -- (unintelligible) where did James Brown come from, Augusta or Macon?
But I know a young civil rights attorney in Macon who --
-- said he -- his mother lives in Los Angeles, and everytime he comes out here he has glowing stories about --
It's good to hear, you know.

That's real good to hear, yeah, because music has broken down a lot of barriers, you know. But guys really had to go through it, the older guys. They couldn't lose their cool. They had to really go through it to really help it, you know, because if they had blown up too much and
lost their cool, it would have set it right back where it was. But they had to go all the way through it.

I don't know. Most of the bands that I worked in though that when we did play the South, we found that we had real good friends on all sides, on both sides. Maybe a few -- a few less on one side or the other but we did have some real good. There was hope all the time because you saw some people who were really, they meant it. They were very sincere. They couldn't do but so much because their hands were tied. Usually it wasn't the people in the high positions who were like that.

But, you know, if enough of them feel like that, eventually it's going to build and be more and more until eventually something comes -- something good comes out of it, you know. I don't think we'd have made it if it wasn't for that type of person being around, you know. Before it was survival of the fittest, you know. A lot of them fell by the wayside. Oh, boy.
